title: Stability
hook: Benedictines vow to stay in one community for life

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first word of Benedict's Rule: listen. Your line was the ear of the heart. Did anyone get to finish a sentence because you waited? Day one thousand one hundred thirteen.

A new monk stands in the chapel in front of the whole community. In his hand is a promise he has written out himself, and he lays it on the altar. Benedict's Rule tells us what goes in it. He promises obedience. He promises to keep turning his life toward God. And he promises something that sounds, to modern ears, almost impossible. He promises to stay. Not to stay a monk in general, anywhere, wherever things feel right. To stay here, with these brothers, under this roof, in this community. No moving on when the abbot gets on his nerves or the brother in the next stall hums off key. The Rule has a Latin word for that promise, and it's today's word: stabilitas.

Stabilitas. Stability. To see why Benedict cared, look at his very first chapter. He describes different kinds of monks, and the ones he's hardest on are the wanderers. They drift from monastery to monastery, a few days here, a few days there, never settling, always guests. In the Rule's picture, they follow their own wishes and never stay long enough for anyone to know them. Benedict's answer is the vow to stay. Later, after a long list of what he calls the tools of the spiritual craft, things like don't return evil for evil, love your enemies, don't give up on God's mercy, he says where those tools get used. The workshop, he says, is the enclosure of the monastery and stability in the community. That's the surprise. Stability isn't a reward for being holy. It's the workbench. In this picture, patience gets learned with people you can't leave, and forgiveness gets tested by staying near the person you need to forgive. Move on every time it gets hard, and the tools never touch the wood. There's an old line in the Bible that sounds like this vow, though it comes from a different story. Ruth, a widow, refuses to leave her mother-in-law, and says, "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge." Stability is that kind of loyalty, given to a place and a people. You may never take a monk's vow. But there may be one hard place you keep wanting to leave.

Here's the practice: stay put in one hard place. Sit where you are, and notice the urge to move: to check the phone, shift your weight, get up for something. Don't follow it. Just stay. Then bring to mind one place, one job, one relationship you'd like to walk out of today. You don't have to fix it. Just picture yourself staying in it a little longer, with your feet on the floor. If you pray, you can bring that place to God by name. The bell holds the time.
Stabilitas. The Benedictine promise to stay with one community, so that the hard work of love has somewhere to happen.
Your line: stay. Today, when you feel the pull to leave a hard moment, a meeting, a talk, a chore, stay five minutes longer than you want to. Day one thousand one hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns make a vow of stability that ties them to a particular community; Benedictine oblates living outside the monastery can take stability as a call to stay faithful to their own family, parish and place.

notes: Rule paraphrased throughout. Chapter 58: the promise of stability, conversatio morum and obedience, written by the novice's hand and placed on the altar in the oratory. Chapter 1: the gyrovagues. Chapter 4 (end): the workshop is the enclosure of the monastery and stability in the community. Please confirm.
The tools listed (not returning evil for evil, loving enemies, never despairing of God's mercy) are from Rule 4; check the paraphrase.
Ruth 1:16 is explicitly framed as a different story with a similar loyalty, not as Benedict's source.
The closing lines are addressed to the listener as a possibility ('there may be'), not a claim.
The index hook says 'for life'; the script says the monk promises to stay with this community and avoids stating 'for life' as a fact. Confirm how strongly to put it.
